current_episode.title: Can I Love My Body and Still Want to Change It?

guest.bio_context: Sarah Denny is a personal trainer with approximately 10 years of training experience and a power lifter. She was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis at age 21 and endometriosis at age 15, which initially led her to avoid exercise. After a doctor's recommendation at age 24, she began working out and eventually pursued personal training as a career, first working at Good Life Fitness for five years before transitioning to online coaching. She is a mother of a child who is almost five years old.

pending_qa.q: What role does exercise play in recovery from serious physical injury and chronic pain conditions?
pending_qa.r: Sarah Denny suffered a massive injury involving sciatica-type pain that lasted almost two years and prevented her from walking, sleeping, cooking, or cleaning. After being prescribed medications that caused weight gain, she prioritized strength training and lifting, which helped her recover from the injury and regain her quality of life. Dr. Rebecca Chase shared a similar experience with a back injury that resolved, after which she also focused on becoming as strong as possible.

pending_qa.q: How did a childhood diagnosis of endometriosis and rheumatoid arthritis influence entry into personal training?
pending_qa.r: Sarah Denny was diagnosed with endometriosis at age 15 and rheumatoid arthritis at age 21, experiences that caused significant body pain. She did not grow up athletic and initially believed exercise was only for weight loss. At age 24, her doctor recommended she start working out to help manage her pain. She signed up for a gym, got on the treadmill, and eventually had a consultation with a personal trainer that changed her trajectory.

pending_qa.q: What early workplace experience motivated a shift from weakness to physical strength?
pending_qa.r: While working at Blockbuster Video, Sarah Denny could not pick up a crate of ice cream from the freezer—a task she had to perform nightly. Her managers and co-workers made fun of her for this weakness, which became a motivator. She wanted to become strong enough to have physical power, which drove her initial commitment to personal training alongside her goal to manage the pain from her health conditions.

pending_qa.q: How did a career transition from paralegal to personal trainer originate?
pending_qa.r: Sarah Denny was working as a paralegal doing condo law, which she found extremely boring and depressing. While at her hairdresser, she broke down about her unhappiness at work, and her hairdresser suggested she pursue her passion for fitness. After that conversation, she reached out to her former personal trainer to ask about certifications, eventually leaving her paralegal job to pursue personal training full-time.

pending_qa.q: What is the difference between body positivity, body neutrality, and being able to love your body while wanting to change it?
pending_qa.r: Sarah Denny explained that body neutrality means having zero opinion about your body, but she does love her body while also having things she would like to change. She noted that body positivity messaging sometimes suggested that loving your body meant you shouldn't want to change it, and vice versa. She advocates for the power of 'and' rather than 'but'—you can love your body and also want to change certain things about it, a perspective she learned in therapy.

pending_qa.q: How should personal trainers approach clients with histories of disordered eating or eating disorders?
pending_qa.r: Sarah Denny shared that she has worked with many clients who suffered from disordered eating patterns. With one client who was deep in an eating disorder, she helped her find a therapist, reframed exercise as a way to get stronger rather than lose weight, and emphasized that nourishing the body is essential for performance. She noted that you cannot lift weights while starving, and that shifting the narrative from weight loss to health and strength is critical for recovery.

pending_qa.q: What does the transition from in-person to online personal training require in terms of coaching skills?
pending_qa.r: Sarah Denny worked at Good Life Fitness for five years before switching to online coaching. She emphasized that online training is harder because you cannot give clients immediate corrective feedback in the moment. You must learn to communicate feedback verbally and allow clients to apply it over time, checking progress the following week. Without in-person training experience, online coaching becomes significantly more challenging.

pending_qa.q: How does diet culture and diet industry messaging from the 1990s continue to influence body image and eating patterns today?
pending_qa.r: Dr. Rebecca Chase noted that she grew up in the 1990s when magazines like Shape featured diet plans under 1,800 calories, and she recently discovered via a DEXA scan that her maintenance calories are 2,500—a significant deficit. This demonstrates how the restrictive messaging of that era created unrealistic expectations that persisted into adulthood and contributed to the normalization of disordered eating patterns.
